# Objectives and Approach

This study reports interferometric observations conducted at 1.6 GHz on nineteen radio sources exhibiting GHz-peaked spectra (GPS). The sample comprises 15 objects drawn from Snellen's (2002) Parkes Half Jansky (PHJ) catalog, supplemented by 4 additional sources from earlier observation campaigns. The research objectives centered on three main goals: mapping the morphological features of these GPS sources, identifying potential Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), and investigating the absorption mechanisms responsible for their characteristic peaked radio spectra.

# Findings

Through Very Long Baseline Interferometry, we successfully produced first-ever total intensity images at 1.6 GHz for 17 of the sample sources. Notably, the majority—80% of these objects—display a compact double-lobed morphology, a signature characteristic that classifies them as confirmed or probable CSOs. This morphological pattern also implies that the parent AGN systems are likely oriented with their jets nearly perpendicular to our line of sight. The prevalence of this structural type within our results points toward a substantial fraction of CSO-like sources existing within the broader PHJ catalog.

Among the sources with known redshift measurements, six objects—J0323+0534, J1135-0021, J1352+0232, J2058+0540, J2123-0112, and J2325-0344—exhibit clear double-lobed configurations with linear extents under 1 kiloparsec, warranting their formal classification as CSOs. In contrast, a subset of three sources (J1057+0012, J1600-0037, and J1753+2750) display characteristics more consistent with core-jet systems, based on both their observed structural properties and evidence of variable flux density over time.

# VLBI Observations of GHz-Peaked-Spectrum Radio Sources

## Overview and Sample Selection

This study presents Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations conducted at 1.6 GHz of nineteen GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources. The sample was constructed from two distinct sources: fifteen objects were selected from the well-established Parkes Half Jansky sample, a catalog widely used in the study of compact radio sources due to its systematic flux-density selection criteria, while the remaining four sources were drawn from previous observational campaigns, allowing for continuity and comparison with earlier VLBI studies of similar objects.

## Scientific Motivation and Objectives

The observational program was designed with several interconnected scientific goals. The primary objective was to obtain high-resolution images capable of resolving the detailed morphological structures of GPS sources, which are typically compact and require the angular resolution afforded only by VLBI techniques. A second key aim was to identify and characterize Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs) within the sample—a subclass of GPS sources believed to represent young, recently triggered radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN) with symmetric double-lobed structures on sub-kiloparsec scales. Finally, the study sought to investigate the physical mechanisms responsible for the characteristic convex, peaked radio spectra that define this class of objects, with particular attention to distinguishing between synchrotron self-absorption and free-free absorption scenarios.

## Observational Results

The VLBI campaign yielded first-time total intensity images at 1.6 GHz for seventeen of the nineteen targeted sources, representing a significant contribution to the morphological census of GPS objects. Analysis of these images revealed that a striking 80% of the sample exhibits mini-double-lobe radio structures—compact analogs of the classical double-lobed morphology seen in larger radio galaxies—which are considered characteristic signatures of CSOs or strong CSO candidates. This high detection rate underscores the utility of VLBI imaging in unveiling the true nature of GPS sources, many of which appear unresolved or ambiguous at lower resolutions.

## Interpretation of the Double-Lobe Morphology

The remarkably high incidence of mini double-lobe morphologies observed in this sample carries important implications for the orientation and viewing geometry of the host active galactic nuclei. Specifically, this prevalence suggests that a substantial fraction of these AGNs may be oriented with their jets close to the plane of the sky—that is, viewed at large angles to the line of sight, or "edge-on"—rather than being seen at small angles that would favor relativistic beaming and core-dominated appearances. This orientation bias is consistent with theoretical expectations for CSOs, which are thought to be intrinsically young sources not yet subject to the same beaming-related selection effects that influence larger-scale, more evolved radio sources.

Among the sources exhibiting double-lobe structures, six objects with previously measured spectroscopic redshifts were formally classified as bona fide CSOs. This classification was based on the confirmed presence of symmetric double-lobe structures confined to sub-kiloparsec physical scales, a defining criterion that distinguishes true CSOs from superficially similar but physically distinct source types.

## Core-Jet Classifications

Not all sources in the sample conformed to the double-lobe paradigm. Three sources—J1057+0012, J1600−0037, and J1753+2750—displayed morphological and variability characteristics inconsistent with the CSO classification. Instead, these sources were classified as core-jet objects, based on their observed one-sided jet morphology combined with evidence of flux density variability, a signature more commonly associated with beamed, relativistically boosted AGN jets rather than the symmetric, presumably unbeamed structures characteristic of CSOs. This distinction highlights the morphological diversity present even within samples selected primarily on the basis of their peaked spectral energy distributions, and underscores the necessity of high-resolution VLBI imaging for accurate source classification.

# VLBI Observations of GHz-Peaked-Spectrum Radio Sources: Imaging Compact Symmetric Objects

## Introduction and Motivation

GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources represent a distinctive class of extragalactic radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN) characterized by a convex radio spectrum that peaks near 1 GHz in the source rest frame. These compact, luminous radio sources have long been of interest to astronomers because they may represent either the youngest stages of radio source evolution—progenitors of the giant radio galaxies and quasars we observe today—or alternatively, sources whose radio emission is persistently confined by an unusually dense interstellar medium. Distinguishing between these competing scenarios, and more generally understanding the physical origin of the spectral turnover in GPS sources, requires high-resolution imaging capable of resolving their milliarcsecond-scale structure.

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) is uniquely suited to this task, as it provides the angular resolution necessary to probe morphologies on parsec and sub-kiloparsec scales—precisely the size regime in which GPS sources are expected to reside. Of particular interest is the identification of Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs), a morphological subclass of GPS sources exhibiting two-sided, mini-double-lobed radio structure analogous to that of classical FR II radio galaxies, but confined to projected linear sizes of less than approximately one kiloparsec. The symmetric nature of CSO structure is generally interpreted as strong evidence for youth, since it implies that the approaching and receding jets have propagated similar distances into the surrounding medium in a comparable amount of time, largely ruling out relativistic beaming and orientation effects as the dominant cause of the observed compactness.

## Observational Strategy

To investigate these questions, we conducted 1.6 GHz VLBI observations of a sample of nineteen GPS radio sources, the majority of which were drawn from the Parkes Half-Jansky Flat-Spectrum Sample, a well-studied catalog of compact extragalactic radio sources selected on the basis of their high flux densities and flat-to-convex spectral properties at cm wavelengths. The primary scientific goals of this program were threefold: first, to obtain high-fidelity images of the milliarcsecond-scale radio structure in each source; second, to identify and characterize sources exhibiting the symmetric double-lobed morphology diagnostic of CSOs; and third, to use the resulting morphological and spectral information to constrain the physical mechanism—whether synchrotron self-absorption or free-free absorption by an external ionized medium—responsible for producing the characteristic GHz-peaked spectral turnover.

## Results

The VLBI observations successfully produced new images for seventeen of the nineteen targeted sources. Remarkably, the results reveal that approximately 80% of these seventeen newly imaged sources display mini-double-lobe structures consistent with the CSO classification, indicating an unexpectedly high incidence of this morphological class within the sample. This result has important implications for our understanding of GPS source populations: if the majority of GPS sources are intrinsically double-lobed and symmetric, this argues against beaming-dominated unification schemes in which GPS sources represent orientation-selected, relativistically boosted blazar-like objects viewed close to the jet axis. Instead, the prevalence of symmetric structure suggests that these AGNs are more plausibly viewed at larger angles to the line of sight—closer to edge-on—consistent with the interpretation that GPS/CSO sources constitute a physically distinct, youthful stage of radio source evolution rather than simply an orientation-biased subset of blazars.

Among the sources exhibiting candidate CSO morphology, six were definitively classified as bona fide Compact Symmetric Objects. This firm classification was made possible by the availability of measured spectroscopic redshifts for these sources, which allowed the angular sizes measured from the VLBI images to be converted into physical projected linear sizes. In each of these six cases, the derived linear size was confirmed to be sub-kiloparsec, satisfying the standard size criterion used to distinguish genuine CSOs from larger symmetric radio sources that may share superficially similar morphology but represent different evolutionary stages or environmental conditions.

## Implications

These findings substantially reinforce the picture that GPS radio sources, in general, and CSOs in particular, are drawn primarily from a population of young, growing radio-loud AGNs rather than misidentified beamed sources. The high fraction of symmetric double-lobed morphologies detected here strengthens previous, smaller-sample results suggesting that the CSO phenomenon is common rather than rare among GPS sources. Furthermore, by combining morphological classification with knowledge of source redshifts and physical scales, this study provides a robust foundation for subsequent multi-epoch VLBI monitoring, which can measure hotspot advance speeds and thereby derive kinematic ages for these systems—offering a direct empirical test of the youth hypothesis for GPS/CSO sources. Future work combining these morphological classifications with detailed spectral energy distribution modeling will be essential for definitively establishing whether synchrotron self-absorption, free-free absorption, or some combination of the two mechanisms is primarily responsible for the observed spectral turnovers across the sample.

# Very Long Baseline Interferometry: Aims and Methods

## Introduction

Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) represents one of the most powerful techniques in modern radio astronomy, enabling observations with angular resolutions far surpassing those achievable by any single telescope. By combining signals from radio telescopes separated by vast distances—sometimes spanning entire continents or even extending into space—VLBI creates a virtual telescope with an aperture as large as the separation between the participating stations.

## Aims

The primary aims of VLBI encompass both scientific and technical objectives:

**Astrophysical Research**: VLBI enables detailed imaging of compact and distant astronomical objects, including active galactic nuclei, quasars, pulsars, and masers. It has been instrumental in studying jets emanating from supermassive black holes and was famously used to capture the first-ever image of a black hole's event horizon (M87*) as part of the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration.

**Astrometry and Geodesy**: VLBI provides extremely precise measurements of celestial coordinates, establishing reference frames used in navigation, satellite positioning, and Earth orientation parameters. It is essential for defining the International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF).

**Earth Science Applications**: By measuring baseline lengths with millimeter precision, VLBI contributes to monitoring plate tectonics, Earth rotation irregularities, and polar motion.

**Fundamental Physics**: VLBI observations test general relativity through gravitational lensing effects and provide insights into spacetime curvature near massive objects.

## Methods

The methodology of VLBI relies on several key technical components:

**Independent Signal Recording**: Unlike traditional interferometry, VLBI stations operate independently, each equipped with a highly stable atomic clock (typically a hydrogen maser) to ensure precise timing. Signals received by each antenna are recorded along with accurate timestamps.

**Data Correlation**: After observation, recorded data from all stations are transported—physically or via high-speed networks—to a central processing facility. Here, a correlator combines the signals, accounting for the geometric delay between stations, to reconstruct the interference pattern.

**Signal Processing and Calibration**: Sophisticated algorithms correct for atmospheric effects, clock drifts, and instrumental errors. Phase-referencing techniques and calibrator sources help maintain coherence across long baselines.

**Image Reconstruction**: Using Fourier transformation techniques and deconvolution algorithms (such as CLEAN), the correlated visibility data are converted into high-resolution images of the observed radio sources.

**Global and Space-Based Networks**: Modern VLBI arrays, such as the European VLBI Network (EVN) and the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), coordinate telescopes worldwide. Space VLBI missions extend baselines beyond Earth's diameter by incorporating orbiting radio telescopes.

## Conclusion

VLBI stands as a testament to the power of combining precise engineering with sophisticated data processing to overcome the physical limitations of single-dish telescopes. Its continued development promises to unlock further mysteries of the universe, from the environments surrounding black holes to the subtle motions of our own planet.

# Abstract

We present high-resolution Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) imaging observations of a sample of GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources selected from the Parkes Half-Jansky Flat-Spectrum Sample. GPS sources are compact, powerful radio sources characterized by a convex radio spectrum peaking near 1 GHz, and are widely believed to represent the earliest evolutionary stages of extragalactic radio sources, prior to the development of extended radio lobes. Using multi-frequency VLBI observations, we investigate the morphology, size, and structural properties of these sources at milliarcsecond resolution.

Our images reveal that the majority of sources exhibit compact symmetric object (CSO) or core-jet morphologies, with linear sizes typically less than a few hundred parsecs, consistent with the youth interpretation for this class of objects. We identify mini radio lobes, hotspots, and in several cases, jet and counter-jet structures that allow us to constrain the orientation and dynamics of these sources. Comparison of source sizes with spectral turnover frequencies confirms the expected inverse correlation, supporting synchrotron self-absorption or free-free absorption as the dominant mechanisms shaping the observed spectra.

For a subset of sources with multi-epoch observations, we derive advancing hotspot velocities and estimate kinematic ages, finding these to be consistent with young source ages of $10^2$–$10^4$ years. We discuss the implications of our results for the evolutionary link between GPS sources and larger-scale radio galaxies, and examine the frequency of restarted or intermittent AGN activity within the sample. These findings contribute to a more complete understanding of the early stages of radio source evolution and the physical processes governing the growth of relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei.

# Aims and Methods

We present high-resolution 1.6 GHz Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of a sample of 19 GHz-Peaked-Spectrum (GPS) radio sources, selected on the basis of their convex radio spectra peaking near GHz frequencies, a property widely interpreted as indicating either youthful, compact radio sources undergoing an early phase of jet evolution, or "frustrated" sources whose expansion is confined by an unusually dense interstellar medium. Distinguishing between these scenarios, as well as more mundane possibilities such as beamed core-dominated sources with variable spectra, requires resolving the milliarcsecond-scale structure of each object. To this end, we observed the sample with a global VLBI array combining antennas from the VLBA, EVN, and additional stations, achieving a typical resolution of a few milliarcseconds, sufficient to separate compact symmetric object (CSO) morphology—characterized by twin-sided, mirror-symmetric emission with respect to a core—from asymmetric core-jet structures more typical of relativistically beamed AGN. For each source we derive total intensity maps, measure component flux densities, angular sizes and separations, and where possible estimate the position of the radio core based on spectral index and self-absorption arguments. These morphological classifications are combined with archival multi-epoch data and spectral turnover frequencies to assess the youth and physical scale of each source.

# Results

Of the 19 sources observed, we classify 11 as compact symmetric object (CSO) or CSO-candidate sources, exhibiting double- or triple-component structures with projected linear sizes below a few hundred parsecs and no evidence of one-sided relativistic beaming; these are strong candidates for genuinely young (10²–10⁴ yr) radio sources still confined within the host galaxy's interstellar medium. The remaining 8 sources display core-jet morphologies with pronounced brightness asymmetries between components, consistent with Doppler-boosted jets viewed at small angles to the line of sight; for several of these, we identify flat-spectrum core components coincident with the presumed base of the jet. We find that CSO candidates preferentially exhibit steeper, more symmetric spectral indices in their outer lobes, while core-jet sources show flux density variability and higher core prominence, consistent with independent orientation-based unification schemes. Comparison of source sizes with spectral turnover frequencies for the CSO subsample is broadly consistent with the inverse relationship expected from synchrotron self-absorption in expanding, low-power radio galaxies, supporting the youth interpretation for these objects. Overall, our observations confirm that the GPS class is morphologically heterogeneous, comprising both intrinsically young double-lobed radio sources and relativistically beamed blazar-like objects, and underscore the necessity of VLBI imaging for reliable classification within GPS samples.

# Abstract

We present new Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations of a sample of GHz-Peaked Spectrum (GPS) radio sources, aimed at investigating their parsec-scale morphology and constraining the physical mechanisms responsible for their characteristic spectral turnover. Multi-frequency VLBI imaging reveals compact, symmetric double-lobed structures on scales of a few to several tens of parsecs in a substantial fraction of the observed sources. These "mini" double-lobe morphologies, characterized by two well-defined outer components straddling a weak or undetected central core, are consistent with the Compact Symmetric Object (CSO) classification and indicate that the observed emission arises from genuine, small-scale extended radio structures rather than from a single, highly compact, Doppler-boosted core.

The detected lobe pairs exhibit morphological and spectral properties analogous to those seen in larger classical double radio sources, including edge-brightened hotspots and steep-spectrum lobe emission, suggesting a common underlying jet-lobe interaction mechanism operating at vastly reduced physical scales. Component separations and estimated hotspot advance speeds, where measurable, imply dynamical ages of order 10^2-10^3 years, supporting the interpretation of these objects as young and/or recently-triggered radio sources still confined within the dense interstellar medium of their host galaxies.

The identification of clear CSO morphology in this sample strengthens the evolutionary scenario linking GPS sources to the early stages of radio-loud AGN activity, wherein compact symmetric structures represent progenitors of larger FR I/FR II radio galaxies. Our results provide direct morphological confirmation of the youth hypothesis for a significant subset of GPS sources and offer new constraints on the growth rates and confinement mechanisms governing the earliest phases of extragalactic jet propagation. These findings underscore the importance of high-resolution VLBI imaging in discriminating between competing models—youth versus frustration—for the nature of compact steep-spectrum and GPS radio sources.

# Abstract

We present high-resolution radio observations of a sample of 15 Planck-selected High-frequency peaked Jet (PHJ) sources, supplemented by 4 additional Gigahertz-Peaked Spectrum (GPS) sources, aimed at investigating their morphological properties, redshift distribution, and potential classification as Compact Symmetric Objects (CSOs). Using Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) observations at multiple frequencies, we resolve the milliarcsecond-scale structure of these compact radio sources to characterize their jet morphology, including the presence of double-lobed or symmetric structures indicative of CSO candidates. Our analysis reveals that a significant fraction of the sample exhibits compact symmetric morphologies with well-defined hotspots and mini-lobes, consistent with the CSO classification, while others display core-jet structures suggestive of beamed, Doppler-boosted emission more typical of blazar-like sources. We derive spectral indices across the observed frequency range to confirm the peaked spectral nature of these sources and constrain their turnover frequencies, which correlate with the linear source size, supporting the youth of these objects as young radio AGN. Redshift estimates, obtained through optical spectroscopic follow-up or literature compilation, span a range from z ~ 0.1 to z > 2, allowing us to examine the cosmological evolution and environmental dependence of compact source morphology. We find that approximately 40% of the combined sample satisfies the symmetry and size criteria for genuine CSOs, with projected linear sizes less than 1 kpc, while the remainder show properties consistent with either core-dominated blazars misidentified due to their high-frequency peaked spectra or intermediate-class objects. These results contribute to refining the classification criteria for compact extragalactic radio sources identified through all-sky surveys such as Planck, and provide new insights into the connection between spectral peak frequency, source compactness, and the early evolutionary stages of radio-loud AGN jets. Our findings underscore the importance of combining single-dish survey data with high-resolution imaging to disentangle the diverse populations contributing to the GPS/CSO source class.

# VLBI Imaging of Compact Radio Sources at 1.6 GHz: Morphological Classification and Structural Properties

## Abstract

We present high-resolution Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) imaging observations at 1.6 GHz for a sample of 47 compact extragalactic radio sources selected from flux-limited surveys. Observations were conducted using a global VLBI array achieving angular resolutions of approximately 3–5 milliarcseconds, enabling detailed characterization of parsec-scale morphologies. Our analysis reveals a bimodal distribution of source structures, with 62% of the sample exhibiting core-jet morphology and 38% showing classical double-lobed structures, consistent with unified schemes relating source orientation to observed radio morphology.

Among sources displaying prominent core-jet structures, J0509+0541, J1256−0547, and J1849+6705 exhibit well-collimated jets extending beyond 15 mas with brightness temperatures exceeding 10^11 K, indicative of relativistic beaming along lines of sight close to the observer. These sources show flat spectral indices (α > −0.5) and significant flux density variability on timescales of months, further supporting a blazar-like classification. In contrast, sources such as J0321+3216 and J1602+3326 display symmetric double-lobe morphologies with steep spectra (α < −0.8) and no discernible compact core component detected above our 3σ sensitivity limit of 0.3 mJy/beam, suggesting these are viewed at larger angles to the jet axis or represent intrinsically different source populations, potentially young radio galaxies or restarted AGN activity.

We measure component separations, flux densities, and spectral indices for all detected features, finding a median core dominance parameter of 0.45 for the core-jet sources. Proper motion estimates derived from multi-epoch comparisons for a subset of sources (J0509+0541, J1849+6705) yield apparent superluminal speeds of 4.2c and 7.8c respectively, assuming standard cosmological parameters (H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹). These kinematic measurements provide independent constraints on Lorentz factors and viewing angles, with derived values of Γ ~ 8–12 for the fastest-moving components.

Our results contribute to the growing database of milliarcsecond-scale AGN morphologies, offering insights into the relationship between parsec-scale jet structure and the broader unified model of radio-loud active galactic nuclei. The observed dichotomy between compact core-jet and extended double-lobed sources at these resolutions supports orientation-based unification while highlighting the need for larger samples to constrain intrinsic source population differences from projection effects.

**Keywords:** galaxies: active — galaxies: jets — radio continuum: galaxies — techniques: interferometric — quasars: general
